title: The services page a two-sided marketplace actually needs
excerpt: List each service in the scarce side's words: the outcome, the boundary, and a next step that joins that side. A grid of vague capabilities does not help.
alt: A glass-walled office corridor with a sofa, a floor lamp, and black pendant lights, the kind of interior a services page should not mistake for the work itself.
caption: A quiet office corridor with a sofa and pendant lights. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What belongs in each block on a marketplace services page?
faqs.answer: Each block needs an outcome the scarce side would notice, a boundary that names at least one thing you will not do, and a next step that joins the side you need first. Use the words that side already uses for the job. If you cannot state those three parts, the item is not ready to publish as a service.

faqs.question: How many services should an early marketplace list?
faqs.answer: Three to five real jobs is usually enough. More than that often means features of one service have been split into separate cards. Order them the way the scarce side meets them: get on the market, get paid, then get help when something goes wrong. Leave off programs you do not run this month.

faqs.question: Why do capability grids fail on a marketplace site?
faqs.answer: Equal tiles hide the boundary and the next step, and they imply every capability matters the same amount. The scarce side needs to see a refusal, such as who carries insurance or which cities you serve, in the same block as the promise. A grid can still look tidy. It should not be the only writing on the card.

markdown:
A two-sided marketplace services page should list the work in the language of the side that has to arrive first. Each offer needs an outcome, a boundary, and a next step, and that step is to join. A grid of vague capabilities gives the team a poster. It does not give a stranger a decision.

The page is not a second homepage and it is not a feature dump from the product spec. It is a short catalog of jobs you will actually do for that side, written so they can tell which job is theirs.

## Write the work in their words

Start from the sentence they would use with a friend. "I need somewhere to fill my empty Tuesday nights." "I need loads that are not a race to the bottom." "I need families who have already been checked." Those sentences are the services. The internal names can stay in the repo.

Translate each sentence into a heading a person can scan. "Fill open tables." "Post a lane and take a rate." "Pick up shifts that are already staffed on the family side." If the heading could be swapped onto a competitor in another category, it is still your vocabulary, not theirs.

Google's people-first content guidance asks whether a page helps someone do what they came to do, and whether it shows knowledge of the subject rather than a rewrite of generic claims. A services page passes that test when a coach, a host, or a carrier can point at one block and say "that is my job." It fails when every block says you are seamless, scalable, and end to end.

Read the headings out loud to someone who does the work and is not on your team. When they correct a word, take the correction. "Gig" may be the word in your deck and an insult in their kitchen. "Shift" may be precise for one market and meaningless in another.

## Outcome, boundary, next step

Give every service the same three parts. The repetition is a kindness. Visitors learn the pattern on the first block and read the rest faster.

The outcome is one sentence in their unit of success. More booked dinners. A trailer that leaves with a rate attached. A week of shifts that pay on Friday. Do not promise a number you cannot trace. "Get discovered" is not an outcome. "Appear in search for your city and your cuisine" is an outcome if that is what the product does.

The boundary is the limit. Which cities. Which credentials. What you will not handle. A host platform that does not provide ingredients should say so in the block, not in a footnote three pages away. A freight board that does not broker the load, and only introduces the two sides, has to say "introduction," because "shipping" will be heard as "you move it."

The next step is the join path for the side you need first, with the same label used on the homepage. "Apply as a host." "List your truck." If a service is not available to that side yet, do not put a button on it. A dead end is worse than a missing card.

Here is the check, in the order a reviewer should use it:

- The heading uses a word that side already says.
- The outcome is visible without a demo.
- The boundary names at least one refusal.
- The button joins the side you are seeding, or the block has no button.

A block that fails any line goes back to the draft. It does not ship as "good enough for launch."

## How many blocks the page can hold

Three to five services is usually the honest count for an early market. More than that and you are listing features of one service as if they were separate businesses. Fewer than that and you may be hiding a second job the scarce side actually came to evaluate.

Group by the job, not by your department. "Trust and safety," "growth," and "community" are how a company org chart talks. "We check licenses," "we send you the first clients in a new city," and "we pay out on Fridays" are services if you truly perform them. If "community" means a Slack you rarely open, it is not a block.

Order the blocks the way the scarce side meets them. First the job that gets them on the market. Then the job that gets them paid. Then the job that protects them when something goes wrong. A visitor who has to reconstruct that sequence from a masonry grid will reconstruct it wrong.

The other side may need one block of its own, clearly labeled, or a link to a separate page. Do not give them half the grid. A page that alternates host services and guest services asks every reader to skip every other card. Skipping is how people miss the boundary that would have saved them a bad signup.

## What a capability grid hides

A grid of icons is tempting because it looks finished. Six tiles, a verb in each, a line of gray text. The team can feel the page is complete in an afternoon. The scarce side learns almost nothing.

Tiles hide boundaries. There is no room for "we do not carry the insurance, you do," so the line becomes "coverage you can trust." Tiles hide the next step. Every tile links to the same signup, or to nowhere. Tiles hide priority. Equal cards say equal importance, which is the same error as two equal buttons on the homepage.

If you want a visual rhythm, keep it, and still write the three parts in each card. An icon can mark the job. It cannot replace the refusal. Designers who have only been handed a brand system will reach for the grid because the grid is in the system. The copy has to be allowed to make the cards uneven. The important service gets more lines. The minor one gets a sentence and a link.

Watch for words that entered from a template: leverage, solutions, ecosystem, stakeholders, seamless. None of them name a job. Replace each one with the noun the side already uses, even if the sentence gets plainer. Plain is the point.

## One worked block

Take a kitchen marketplace that needs hosts before diners will browse. A finished block can read like this.

Heading: Host a dinner at your table.

Outcome: Set a date, a menu, and a price. Diners book the seats. You cook. We send the payout after the night runs.

Boundary: We list dinners in three cities. You provide the kitchen, the food, and a menu that matches what you can cook for eight. We do not supply ingredients, and we do not staff the evening. If you cancel inside 48 hours, the diner is refunded and the date comes off your calendar.

Next step: Apply as a host. Have a kitchen address and a sample menu ready. We write back within two business days.

That block is longer than a tile. It is also the first time a careful cook can tell whether the offer fits a weeknight. The same shape works for a carrier, a clinician, or a tutor. Change the nouns. Keep the three parts.

If you do not yet run the payout or the refund the way the block describes, do not publish the block. Describe the manual version you will actually perform. "The founder sends the payout by Friday" is a respectable early service. A polished sentence about "automated disbursements" is a future product wearing a present-tense costume.

## Services the page should refuse

Some requests will arrive from the team, from an investor, or from a deck that has a slide called "platform." Put them through the same three parts. If you cannot name an outcome the scarce side would notice this month, the item is not a service yet.

Typical refusals:

- A "community" with no host, no cadence, and no reason to show up.
- An API for a side that does not have a developer.
- A loyalty program before you have repeat jobs.
- A second product that solves your churn model and not their Tuesday.

Leaving these off the page is a product decision the website makes visible. The page gets quieter. The market gets easier to understand. You can add a service the week it becomes real, with the same three parts, instead of launching a grid you will spend a year apologizing for.

Match the services page to the pricing page in the same editing pass. If the host block promises a payout after the night runs, the price has to say when that payout leaves and what fee was taken. If the carrier block says you only introduce the two sides, the price cannot read like a brokerage margin you never named. The scarce side will open both pages, often in two tabs, and a contradiction is louder there than it was in the doc.

The page after this one should answer who stands behind those promises. A service with no person attached is still a brochure. That is [how a two-sided marketplace should write an about page](/blog/how-a-two-sided-marketplace-should-write-an-about-page).

If you want to walk a draft of those blocks with someone who builds the page as well as the interface, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min).
